leads.name: Treurbeuk (Begraafplaats Daalseweg, right of the entrance)

location.address: Right of the entrance gate, Begraafplaats Daalseweg, Nijmegen

leads.why_a_lead: Fails only the two-independent-source bar, not any hard rule. LRMB register (nr 1687753, status 3/monumentaal, n_trees=1, tree-level coordinates) is a strong single source: single weeping beech, right of the cemetery's entrance gate, on Rijksmonument grounds (Begraafplaats Daalseweg, aanleg monument nr 522938), free public Catholic cemetery, open daytime hours, owner category religieuze instantie. Could not find a second independent source naming THIS specific tree. Direct fetches of nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Begraafplaats_Daalseweg, dodenakkers.nl, nijmeegsglorie.nl/daalseweg, begraafplaatsennijmegen.nl and groenerfgoedzorg.nl all confirm the cemetery's Rijksmonument design (two crossing paths lined with RED beeches meeting at a crucifix) but none of them, read directly, name a weeping beech or any tree specifically at the entrance gate. A WebSearch AI summary twice asserted 'large weeping beeches at the entrance gate' and 'about thirty trees on the municipal monumental list including a weeping beech among beech trees from before 1900, ash, elm, maple, yew, and a beech with an ingrown gravestone', but repeated attempts to find the underlying page that actually says this failed (rijksmonumenten.nl/monument/522938 hung on two separate fetch attempts, both via WebFetch and via curl -m 20 with a browser user agent, so it is a candidate for the fetch blocklist). Per BRIEF_RESEARCH.md's rule that a search summary is a lead, never a source, that claim is recorded here rather than used to verify the tree. Next pass: try rijksmonumenten.nl again with a longer gap, or find the municipality's own monumentale-bomen map/dataset entry for this coordinate (opendata.nijmegen.nl bomen dataset, WFS/CSV, ~60,000 municipal trees total, not yet queried for this specific point).

leads.name: Zilveresdoorn (Sumatraplein 24)
leads.why_a_lead: Weak on both count and evidence. Register status is 2 (potentieel/potential candidate), the lowest standing in this batch, not the confirmed-monumentaal status 3 the other entries carry: the register itself is not yet calling this one designated. It is an ordinary municipal street tree (setting 'weg') of a common species with no recorded girth, no distinguishing history and no news coverage found (checked for kapvergunning/felling-permit disputes, a common way an ordinary tree gets a second source in Dutch local media: none found). Searched the Nijmegen-Oost neighbourhood association's own page about local monumental trees (nijmegen-oost.nl/berichten/leuk-wat-zijn-de-monumentale-bomen-in-jouw-buurt, fetched directly via curl with a browser user-agent after WebFetch 403'd) and it does not mention Sumatraplein or a silver maple at all. No second source found; does not yet clear either the evidence bar or a case for being remarkable beyond the register listing it as a potential candidate.

leads.name: Witte paardenkastanje Landhuis Brakkenstein

location.address: Landgoed Brakkenstein, bij het landhuis, Nijmegen

leads.why_a_lead: Fails only the two-independent-source bar. LRMB register (nr 1681242, status 3/monumentaal, n_trees=1, tree-level coordinates, owner gemeente, visitable=ja, visible=ja) names this specifically as standing 'bij het landhuis' (by the manor house), distinct from the estate's beech-lined avenues and its northwest beech circle. Checked directly: the Rijksmonument description of Landgoed Brakkenstein (monumentenregister.cultureelerfgoed.nl/complexen/522926, fetched directly) and of Park Brakkenstein (monumenten.nl/monument/522933) describe the park's lane structure and star-forest layout in general terms but name no individual specimen tree by the villa. Also checked directly: eveliendemey.nl/project/park-brakkenstein (a landscape-design portfolio piece on the park's restoration), noviomagus.nl/Vrij/Brakkenstein/BrakkensteinCat.html (local history), landgoedbrakkesteyn.nl (the venue's own site) and nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landgoed_Brakkenstein: none name a chestnut or beech specifically by the house. A separate dead-tree report (mijnbrakkenstein.nl/berichten/monumentale-boom-gesneefd) concerns a different tree entirely, a sweet/tame chestnut (tamme kastanje, Castanea sativa, not this white horse chestnut / Aesculus) at 'de Drie Huizen', a different named site on the same estate, so it does NOT block this candidate; recorded here so a future pass does not confuse the two. Nothing found confirms or contradicts this tree's continued existence; recorded as a lead rather than delivered because the two-source bar is unmet, not because of any doubt about the tree itself.

leads.name: Beuk Landhuis Brakkenstein

location.address: Landgoed Brakkenstein, bij het landhuis, Nijmegen

leads.why_a_lead: Same finding and same searches as nr 1681242 immediately above (essentially the same spot, ~15m apart, both 'bij het landhuis'): a single, specific, tree-level register entry with no news, heritage-description or local-history source naming this individual tree. NOT the same entry as the previously blocked Beukenlaan avenue tree (nr 1681243, at 51.820303,5.872431, roughly 230m away and explicitly labelled by the register as 'Beukenlaan nabij restaurant', a different named location on the estate): this one's place field reads 'bij het landhuis', matching the chestnut beside it rather than the avenue, so the avenue/whole-wood exclusion that blocked 1681243 does not automatically apply here. Still, no independent source distinguishes it as a visually singular specimen (girth, plaque, planting story) the way BRIEF_RESEARCH.md would want before treating a beech standing near a lane-lined park as clearly its own collectible point rather than another lane tree; flagged for a future pass to check on the ground or via a dated aerial/satellite crown check (PDOK) whether it stands free of the lane structure. Recorded as a lead on the two-source bar, not blocked.

leads.name: Bruine beuk (kerkplein, Petruskerk, Hees)
leads.why_a_lead: Fails only the two-source bar. LRMB register (nr 1680527, status 5, reason monumentaal, n_trees=1, tree-level coordinates, owner_category religieuze instantie, visitable=ja, visible=onbekend) names a single copper beech on the small square at Schependomlaan/Korte Bredestraat in Hees, where Nijmegen's old village church, the Petruskerk, stands (directly fetched: woneninnijmegen.blog/2026/05/02/schependomlaan and nijmeegsglorie.nl/index.php/schependomlaan both confirm the church sits 'aan een pleintje', a small square, at exactly this corner; the tower is on Korte Bredestraat, the church and consistory on Schependomlaan, matching the register's own two-street address). Note the church itself is a former Dutch Reformed (Protestant) building, sold to a private owner in 2020 per the same blog (rented since to Bethel Tempel); this does not by itself disqualify the SQUARE it stands on, which reads as an open village plein rather than an enclosed churchyard, but it is worth flagging since the register's owner_category 'religieuze instantie' may predate that 2020 sale. STATUS ANOMALY, recorded rather than acted on: this entry carries status=5, while its immediate neighbour nr 1680526 (15m away, same square) carries status=3, though both share reason='monumentaal'; checked the register's own status distribution (data/registers/netherlands-lrmb.json) and status 3 and 5 both pair with 'monumentaal' in the large majority of entries nationwide (7,966 and 3,375 respectively), so this looks like a batch or source-provenance code rather than a quality signal, but no schema documentation was found to confirm what the codes mean. No independent source naming THIS beech specifically was found: a monumentaltrees.com page exists for this exact square (title 'Gewone platanen bij de Petruskerk in Nijmegen', URL monumentaltrees.com/nl/nld/gelderland/nijmegen/32428_petruskerk/, found via WebSearch) but the page itself returned HTTP 403 on two direct fetch attempts (curl with a browser user-agent, and WebFetch), matching this host's known automated-fetch block; per BRIEF_RESEARCH.md a search result's title is not treated as a verified fact, only as a pointer, so this is recorded as an unopened lead for a session with real browser access, not as a second source. Also tried and hung (two attempts each, now candidates for the fetch blocklist): reliwiki.nl/index.php/Nijmegen,_Schependomlaan_83_-_Petruskerk (curl -m 20, exit 28 both times) and the municipality's own WFS endpoint services.nijmegen.nl/geoservices/extern_OpenData/ows (typeName extern_kaartviewer_GRN_BOMEN_MON), which would have been the strongest independent corroboration (Nijmegen's own municipal monumental-tree map, distinct in provenance from the national LRMB/Bomenstichting register per degroenestad.nl's description of it) but hung past the TLS handshake on both attempts.

leads.name: Gewone plataan (kerkplein, Petruskerk, Hees)
leads.why_a_lead: Same square as nr 1680527 immediately above, about 15m away, same finding: LRMB register (status 3/monumentaal, n_trees=1, tree-level coordinates, owner_category religieuze instantie, visitable=ja, visible=onbekend) is a strong single source, the square itself is independently confirmed as a real 'pleintje' beside the old Petruskerk (see the copper beech entry above for the two directly-fetched local-history sources), but no independent source names this specific plane tree. The monumentaltrees.com page found for this square is titled 'Gewone platanen bij de Petruskerk' (plural 'platanen'), which is suggestive that more than one plane tree is recorded there, but the page 403'd on both fetch attempts (see the beech entry above for the exact hosts and attempts) so nothing beyond the title could be confirmed, and per the search-summary rule a title is a pointer, not a source. A future session with real browser access to monumentaltrees.com (per BRIEF_RESEARCH.md, viewing their pages is an allowed corroboration use, never bulk scraping) would likely close both this and the beech above in minutes.

leads.name: Bruine beuk (RK Kerk, Dennenstraat, Hees)

location.address: RK Kerk, Op de grens van Dennenstr 121 en 125, Hees (Nijmegen)

leads.why_a_lead: The oldest candidate checked this pass (roughly 225-275 years) and fails only the two-source bar. LRMB register (nr 1680519, status 3/monumentaal, n_trees=1, tree-level coordinates, owner_category religieuze instantie, visitable=ja, visible=ja) places a single copper beech at the boundary of Dennenstraat 121 and 125, which directly-fetched sources identify as the Sint Antonius Abtkerk (the Catholic parish church of Hees, Dennenstraat 125, with its rectory at 121): kennis.cultureelerfgoed.nl/index.php/Monumenten/31204 (Rijksmonument description, current building by Cuypers, 1879-1880) and nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonius_Abtkerk_(Nijmegen) both confirm the address and the building's history but neither mentions any tree at all. mariakapelvinden.nl/geschiedenis-van-de-antonius-abtkerk-in-hees (directly fetched, a long parish-history piece) confirms the site has centuries of continuous religious use predating the current 1880 building (a 16th-century predecessor church, a 'kerkschuur' rebuilt in 1826, and reference to an even older 'voormalig kerkhof' at the sister church in Hees), which makes a beech planted 1750-1800 on this ground plausible (it would predate the current building by roughly a century, standing on what was already old church land) but this is context, not a source naming the tree itself. Tried and hung (fetch blocklist candidate, curl -m 20, exit 28, two attempts): reliwiki.nl/index.php/Nijmegen,_Dennenstraat_125_-_Antonius_Abt. Tried and empty of tree content: nijmeegsglorie.nl/index.php/dennenstraat (fetched fine, no mention of 'beuk' or 'boom' anywhere on the page). Recorded as a lead, not blocked: nothing found contradicts the tree, the register gives a genuine tree-level pin on a plausible old churchyard site, it is simply unconfirmed by a second source this pass.

blocked.name: Beuk (Beukenlaan, Landgoed Brakkestein)
blocked.reason: Not a collectible point. Register place field itself reads "Beukenlaan nabij restaurant, Landg. Brakkestein": this stands on one of the beech-lined avenues of Brakkestein's 18th-century sterrenbos (star forest) layout. The Rijksmonument description of Park Brakkenstein (monumenten.nl/monument/522933, fetched directly) states the lanes are largely planted with beech trees ('De lanen zijn grotendeels beplant met beukenbomen'), names a specific beech avenue connecting the two far points of the diamond-shaped grounds, and gives no individual tree special recognition; a separate circle of old beeches exists in the park's northwest corner (a different feature, not this register entry). Independent sources (Digitale Huis 'Sterrenbossen in en om Nijmegen', via WebSearch summary only, page itself 403'd) corroborate that the beeches along the lanes are collectively ~250-300 years old from the original planting, i.e. this register entry is one of a run of similar-aged, similar-looking beeches along a lane rather than a distinguishable individual, the same avenue/whole-wood exclusion BRIEF_RESEARCH.md names explicitly. Planted_band 1700-1750 would make it (if it were a valid standalone entry) the oldest candidate in this batch, so it is recorded here rather than discarded in case a future pass finds it is in fact visually distinct from its neighbours (a girthier trunk, a plaque) that would let it re-qualify.

blocked.name: Mammoetboom Park Leeuwenstein, Nijmegen
blocked.reason: DEAD. This tree fell in the storm of 18 January 2018. Two independent sources, both fetched directly (not summaries): dewester.info/ideeen-gezocht-voor-gesneuvelde-mammoetboom (a 2018 local-news piece titled 'Ideas sought for the fallen mammoth tree', stating 'De storm op 18 januari 2018 joeg ook over de Wolfskuil. In park Leeuwenstein op de grens met het Waterkwartier, ging een hele oude boom, een sequoia, omver', i.e. a very old sequoia in Park Leeuwenstein fell over in that storm, on the Wolfskuil/Waterkwartier border, matching this tree's location); and woneninnijmegen.blog/2023/08/16/park-leeuwenstein (fetched directly, an Aug 2023 post listing the park's trees, stating plainly 'Helaas zijn de 2 grootste bomen afgelopen jaren verloren gegaan: De 24 meter hoge mammoetboom', i.e. the park's 24-metre mammoth tree is one of its 2 largest trees lost in recent years; the same post separately notes a 25.6m swamp cypress/moerascipres also fell in the January 2018 storm, so the park lost two large exotic conifers, not one, and this register entry (n_trees=1, the only mammoetboom the register lists for this park) is the mammoth tree specifically, not the cypress). No source suggests a replacement has been planted at this coordinate. Per hard rule ('we doen niet aan dode bomen') and BRIEF_RESEARCH.md's bar 1, a tree known to be dead is never delivered as a live entry.
